title: Why I Declined the Unpaid Recruitment Project
script: Narrator: [thoughtful] After two interviews for a marketing role, the company sent me a final assessment.
Narrator: The email asked for a complete campaign strategy, twelve advertisement ideas, and a detailed budget for a product they planned to launch next month.
Narrator: [carefully] It said the task should take two hours, but producing work at that level would require much longer.
Narrator: I wanted the job, so my first instinct was to cancel my weekend and complete everything.
Narrator: [reflective] Then I noticed that candidates had to transfer all rights to the company, whether or not they were hired.
Narrator: The assignment looked less like a short skills test and more like useful commercial work collected without payment.
Narrator: [honestly] I replied politely and asked what skill each section measured, how submissions would be protected, who would view them, and whether the company would use candidate ideas.
Narrator: I offered alternatives: a smaller fictional case, a timed discussion of a previous anonymized project, or a paid trial with clear terms.
Narrator: [seriously] The recruiter said every candidate had received the same task and nobody else had objected.
Narrator: Equal treatment did not answer the questions about time, accessibility, confidentiality, ownership, or real business use.
Narrator: [gently] I also avoided sending examples that contained former clients’ private information. I described my reasoning without exposing work I had no right to share.
Narrator: Two days later, the company shortened the assessment to a fictional one-page brief and removed the transfer of rights.
Narrator: [encouraging] I completed that version, although I did not assume the change guaranteed a fair workplace.
Narrator: During the final conversation, I asked how performance would be evaluated and requested the criteria in writing.
Narrator: [sincere] I eventually accepted another position whose process used structured interviews and a limited paid exercise.
Narrator: Declining the original assignment felt risky, but it showed me that recruitment tests should be proportionate to the role and should not turn applicants’ need for work into free production.
Narrator: [thoughtful] Candidates may have different legal protections, so a difficult case may also require local professional advice, not only a personal email.

quiz.question: Why did the assessment appear commercially useful?
options: It requested a launch-ready strategy, advertisements, and budget
quiz.explanation: The task resembled real production work.

quiz.question: What clause increased the narrator’s concern?
options: Candidates transferred all rights even if not hired

quiz.question: What alternatives did the narrator offer?
options: A smaller fictional case, an anonymized discussion, or a paid trial
quiz.explanation: The options could test skill more proportionately.

quiz.question: Why was “everyone gets the same task” insufficient?
options: Consistency did not resolve burden, access, confidentiality, ownership, or use
quiz.explanation: A uniform process can still have design problems.

quiz.question: What lesson does the narrator draw?
options: The longest task selects the best worker
Recruitment tests should assess skills without extracting disproportionate free work
quiz.explanation: Proportionality and purpose guide fair assessment.

quiz.question: Why did the two-hour estimate matter?
options: It understated the realistic burden of launch-ready work
The budget was two hours late
quiz.explanation: Estimated and actual effort affected fairness.

quiz.question: What privacy boundary did the narrator keep?
options: The recruiter received every old file
Former clients’ confidential work was not sent as proof of skill
quiz.explanation: A portfolio request does not cancel prior duties.

quiz.question: Why did the shorter fictional task improve the process?
options: It could test reasoning with less extraction of real commercial value
quiz.explanation: The revision better matched assessment purpose.

quiz.question: What did the narrator request at the final conversation?
quiz.explanation: Criteria make the decision more understandable.

quiz.question: Why is local advice mentioned?
options: Marketing tests require a lawyer everywhere
Legal protections and contract rights differ by place and case
quiz.explanation: The text avoids universal legal claims.
